The filter panel on a product listing opens by animating its

from 0 to 280px, and the product grid beside it re-wraps to make room. On the designer's laptop it looks fine; on a budget phone it stutters. We rebuilt it with 1,500 product rows and traced the 300 ms transition in headless Chromium 156. Unthrottled, each frame spent about 4 ms in layout. With the CPU slowed 4x through the DevTools protocol, each layout took 24 to 50 ms across three runs, longer than a whole frame, and only 5 to 9 layout passes fit in the 300 ms instead of 18 or 19. The same panel sliding in with
The belief: every CSS change costs about the same, because after any change the browser simply repaints the page.

It's an easy model to hold. On a fast machine both versions of the panel look smooth, and each is one line of CSS. Developers say "repaint" for any visual update, and the Elements panel shows a style change the same way whatever property it touches. The difference only shows up when a slow device has to do the expensive version 60 times a second.
Five stages, run only as far as needed

Layout has no fixed price. web.dev notes that one element's layout can affect others, so the browser may have to check the rest of the page. MDN calls the first pass layout and every later recalculation a reflow. Moving a fixed drawer with
cost a fraction of a millisecond of layout per frame in our run; widening the panel resized the grid of 1,500 wrapping rows beside it, and layout took about 4 ms per frame.

That matters because of the frame budget. At 60 Hz the browser has 16.66 ms per frame, and web.dev advises finishing your own work within about 10 ms, since the browser needs the rest. Miss it and frames are dropped: that's

content.text: The fix changes the design a little: the panel now slides over the grid instead of pushing it. That's usually the right trade for a panel that opens and closes. If the grid really must make room, let it reflow once, after the panel has opened, not on every frame of the motion.

items.text: Every frame can run up to five stages: JavaScript, Style, Layout, Paint and Composite, and a change runs only those it needs.
Geometry changes re-run layout and paint; appearance-only changes skip layout;
